name: Nehru jacket

lead:
The Nehru jacket is a tailored, hip-length coat with a stand-up mandarin collar and a row of buttons from neck to hem, modelled on the longer Indian achkan and sherwani. It is named for Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, who is associated with the style.
For appearance, the lapel-free design gives a sleek vertical line and keeps attention on the face and neck. It was marketed in Europe and America in the mid-1960s and had a brief fashion wave there; it remains in use in formal wear in South Asia and in contemporary menswear.

paras: It is worn over a shirt, kurta or roll-neck as a suit-alternative jacket, in tailored, often slim cuts, with matching trousers as a 'Nehru suit' or as a contrasting layer. Fabrics range from khadi cotton to wool and silk.
There are no health risks. Fit matters: the stand collar sits close to the neck, so shoulder fit and collar height are the details tailors adjust.

angle.text: The jacket gives a sharp vertical line and a collar that frames the neck, offering a formal option that differs from the lapel suit. It is worn as an outfit choice, so the effect is on overall presentation.

lead: The Nehru jacket is a hip-length, tailored coat with a mandarin (stand-up) collar and a front that follows the longer Indian achkan or sherwani.[1] It is a variation of the Jodhpuri coat and is often made from khadi, hand-woven cloth.[1]

As a style choice, it replaces the lapel-and-tie look of a Western suit with a single clean vertical line of buttons and a collar that frames the neck. People wear it to look formal and polished with a minimalist silhouette.

The jacket became popular in India during Nehru's premiership from 1947 to 1964, although Wikipedia notes he himself preferred the knee-length achkan or sherwani rather than the shorter jacket that carries his name.[1] In the mid-1960s it was marketed in Europe and America and was briefly fashionable there, helped by wearers such as Sammy Davis Jr. and the Beatles.[1]

paras: The garment is hip-length with a standing collar and a central button front.[1] The collar form is traced by an AI-generated encyclopedia to Qing-dynasty Chinese dress, which it says reached the Indian subcontinent through trade, and the jacket's longer relatives, the achkan and sherwani, to Mughal-era formal coats.[2]

Wikipedia describes the Nehru jacket as a variant of the Jodhpuri coat and notes the name came into wide use only after the 1940s; before that, it was called a closed-neck coat in Hindustani.[1] Under the Swadeshi movement and Gandhi's push for khadi, nationalists favoured Indian garments over Western suits.[2]

Nehru wore the achkan through his premiership, which ran from 1947 to 1964.[1][2] In the mid-1960s, Western retailers marketed a shorter version as the 'Nehru jacket'. It was briefly popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s, with attention from mod minimalism, interest in other cultures, and celebrity wearers.[1]
Later wearers include Manmohan Singh, who wore a Nehru-style jacket over a suit in 2011, and Time magazine included it in a 2012 list of political fashion statements.[1]
The entry appears in style-focused material as an alternative formal option.

timeline.event: The term 'Nehru jacket' comes into wide use; earlier the style was called a closed-neck coat.[1]
Nehru serves as prime minister; the style is popularised during this period.[1]
Marketed in Europe and America as the Nehru jacket.[1]
Brief Western fashion popularity, with the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr. among wearers.[1]
Time lists it among political fashion statements.[1]
